On Graham’s rearrangement conjecture

Huy Tuan Pham ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, California Institute for Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125. Email: htpham@caltech.edu. Research supported by a Clay Research Fellowship.    Lisa Sauermann ††thanks: Institute for Applied Mathematics, University of Bonn, Germany. Email: sauermann@iam.uni-bonn.de. Research supported by the DFG Heisenberg Program.
Abstract

Graham conjectured in 1971 that for any prime pp, any subset S⊆ℤp∖{0}S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}\setminus\{0\} admits an ordering s1,s2,…,s|S|s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{|S|} where all partial sums s1,s1+s2,…,s1+s2+⋯+s|S|s_{1},s_{1}+s_{2},\dots,s_{1}+s_{2}+\dots+s_{|S|} are distinct. We prove this conjecture for all subsets S⊆ℤp∖{0}S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}\setminus\{0\} with |S|≤p1−α|S|\leq p^{1-\alpha} and |S||S| sufficiently large with respect to α\alpha, for any α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1). Combined with earlier results, this gives a complete resolution of Graham’s rearrangement conjecture for all sufficiently large primes pp.

1 Introduction

Given an abelian group GG and a subset S⊆GS\subseteq G, a valid ordering of SS is an ordering s1,s2,…,s|S|s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{|S|} of the elements of SS such that all partial sums s1,s1+s2,…,s1+s2+⋯+s|S|s_{1},s_{1}+s_{2},\dots,s_{1}+s_{2}+\dots+s_{|S|} are distinct.

Valid orderings have been a subject of a number of works in combinatorics and group theory. The main subject of this paper is the a conjecture, called Graham’s rearrangement conjecture, which was posed by Graham [7, p. 36] in 1971 and later reiterated by Erdős and Graham [6, p. 95].

Conjecture 1.1.

Any subset S⊆ℤp∖{0}S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}\setminus\{0\} admits a valid ordering.

Graham’s rearrangement conjecture has attracted a lot of interest over the past few years. Bedert and Kravitz [3] showed that the conjecture holds true for small sets SS, namely for |S|≤exp⁡((log⁡p)1/4)|S|\leq\exp((\log p)^{1/4}), improving an earlier result of Kravitz [9] and an observation of Sawin [12]. Müyesser and Pokrovskiy [10] showed that the conjecture holds for very large SS of size |S|≥(1−o⁡(1))​p|S|\geq(1-o(1))p. Bucić, Frederickson, Müyesser, Pokrovskiy and Yepremyan [4] showed an approximate version of the conjecture, where all but o⁡(|S|)o(|S|) many partial sums are guaranteed to be distinct. Recently, Bedert, Bucić, Kravitz, Montgomery and Müyesser [2] showed that the conjecture holds true for large sets SS, namely for |S|≥p1−c|S|\geq p^{1-c} for a small positive constant cc.

The main result of this paper is the following theorem, which shows that Graham’s rearrangement conjecture holds for all S⊆ℤp∖{0}S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}\setminus\{0\} with Cα≤|S|≤p1−αC_{\alpha}\leq|S|\leq p^{1-\alpha}, for any α>0\alpha>0 (with a suitable constant Cα>0C_{\alpha}>0 depending on α\alpha).

Theorem 1.2.

For any 0<α<10<\alpha<1, there exists a constant Cα>0C_{\alpha}>0 such that the following holds. Let pp be a prime and let S⊆ℤp∖{0}S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}\setminus\{0\} be a subset with Cα≤|S|≤p1−αC_{\alpha}\leq|S|\leq p^{1-\alpha}. Then there exists a valid ordering of SS, i.e. there is an ordering s1,s2,…,s|S|s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{|S|} of the elements of SS such that all partial sums s1,s1+s2,…,s1+s2+⋯+s|S|s_{1},s_{1}+s_{2},\dots,s_{1}+s_{2}+\dots+s_{|S|} are distinct.

Together with the earlier results discussed above, this completely settles Graham’s rearrangement conjecture for all sufficiently large primes pp.

Unlike previous results towards Graham’s rearrangement conjecture, employing structural additive combinatorial results, or graph-theoretic arguments relying on suitable notions of expansion and the absorption method, our proof is inherently probabilistic, relying on anticoncentration estimates on sums of random subsets of SS of a given size. More precisely, we prove the following anticoncentration result, which is an important input for our proof of Theorem 1.2.

Theorem 1.3.

There exists an absolute constant C>0C>0 such that the following holds. Let pp be a prime, let S⊆ℤpS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p} be a subset of size |S|≥2|S|\geq 2, and let mm be an integer with C​log⁡|S|≤m≤10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|C\log|S|\leq m\leq 10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|. Now, let R⊆SR\subseteq S be a uniformly random subset of SS of size mm, and let Σ⁡(R)=∑x∈Rx∈ℤp\Sigma(R)=\sum_{x\in R}x\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} be the sum of the elements of RR. Then

maxz∈ℤpℙ[Σ(R)=z]≤1p+C|S|​m.\max_{z\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z]\leq\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C}{|S|\sqrt{m}}.

In our proof of Theorem 1.3, we represent a uniformly random subset RR of size mm by first partitioning SS randomly into mm parts of roughly equal size, and then choose a uniformly random element from each part. To understand the anticoncentration, given a fixed partition, we employ Fourier analytic ideas similar to the work of Nguyen and Vu [11] on the inverse Littlewood–Offord problem. The key new step in the proof is the use of suitable concentration estimates to relate certain quantities involving the random partition of SS to their deterministic analogs.

In order to also handle the case where mm is larger than the upper bound assumed in Theorem 1.3, we use the following corollary of Theorem 1.3.

Corollary 1.4.

For any 0<ε<10<\varepsilon<1 There exists a constant Cε′>0C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}>0 such that the following holds. Let pp be a prime, let S⊆ℤpS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p} be a subset of size |S|≥2|S|\geq 2, and consider a positive integer m≤(1−ε)​|S|m\leq(1-\varepsilon)|S|. Now, let R⊆SR\subseteq S be a uniformly random subset of SS of size mm, and let Σ⁡(R)=∑x∈Rx∈ℤp\Sigma(R)=\sum_{x\in R}x\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} be the sum of the elements of RR. Then

maxz∈ℤpℙ[Σ(R)=z]≤1p+Cε′​log⁡|S||S|​m.\max_{z\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z]\leq\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m}}.

Roughly speaking, our proof of Theorem 1.2 proceeds as follows. Starting from a random ordering of SS, we perform local adjustments for every zero-sum segment (flipping the endpoint of the segment with another later element nearby in the ordering). Using the anticoncentration bounds in Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 1.4, we show that this way we can obtain a valid ordering of SS.

Beside the setup of the cyclic group in Graham’s rearrangement conjecture, valid orderings have also been studied in other groups. Alspach [1, 5] conjectured an analog of Graham’s rearrangement conjecture in arbitrary finite abelian groups. We believe that our argument may generalize to other abelian groups as well, and plan to return Alspach’s conjecture in future work.

Notation.

For a prime pp, and any subset S⊆ℤpS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we write Σ⁡(S)=∑x∈Sx∈ℤp\Sigma(S)=\sum_{x\in S}x\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} for the sum of the elements in SS. All logarithms are to base ee, unless specified otherwise.

Organization.

After some preliminaries in Section 2, we will prove our anticoncentration result, Theorem 1.3, in Section 3. In Section 4, we deduce some corollaries of the anticoncentration result, in particular Corollary 1.4 and an anticoncentration result for a chain of random subsets of given sizes. Finally, we give the proof of out main result, Theorem 1.2, in Section 5, using the anticoncentration results in Section 4.

2 Preliminaries

For y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}, let us define ‖y‖ℤ:=minz∈ℤ⁡|y−z|\|y\|_{\mathbb{Z}}:=\min_{z\in\mathbb{Z}}|y-z| to be the distance of yy to the closest integer (and note that ‖y‖ℤ≤1\|y\|_{\mathbb{Z}}\leq 1 for all y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}).

Fact 2.1.

For all y1,…,yk∈ℝy_{1},\dots,y_{k}\in\mathbb{R}, we have

‖y1+⋯+yk‖ℤ2≤k⋅(‖y1‖ℤ2+⋯+‖yk‖ℤ2).\|y_{1}+\dots+y_{k}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}\leq k\cdot(\|y_{1}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}+\dots+\|y_{k}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}).
Proof.

Let zi∈ℤz_{i}\in\mathbb{Z} be such that ‖yi‖ℤ=|yi−zi|\|y_{i}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}=|y_{i}-z_{i}|. We then have

‖y1+⋯+yk‖ℤ≤|(y1+⋯+yk)−(z1+⋯+zk)|=|∑i=1k(yi−zi)|≤∑i=1k|yi−zi|=∑i=1k‖yi‖ℤ.\|y_{1}+\dots+y_{k}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}\leq|(y_{1}+\dots+y_{k})-(z_{1}+\dots+z_{k})|=\Bigg|\sum_{i=1}^{k}(y_{i}-z_{i})\Bigg|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{k}|y_{i}-z_{i}|=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\|y_{i}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}.

By Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, we can then conclude that

‖y1+⋯+yk‖ℤ2≤(∑i=1k‖yi‖ℤ)2≤k⋅(‖y1‖ℤ2+⋯+‖yk‖ℤ2).∎\|y_{1}+\dots+y_{k}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}\leq\Bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\|y_{i}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}\Bigg)^{2}\leq k\cdot(\|y_{1}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}+\dots+\|y_{k}\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}).\qed
Fact 2.2.

For any y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}, we have

1−20​‖y‖ℤ2≤cos⁡(2​π​y)≤1−2​‖y‖ℤ2.1-20\|y\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}\leq\cos(2\pi y)\leq 1-2\|y\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}.
Proof.

Note that all of the terms in the inequality are 11-periodic functions of yy, which are furthermore symmetric around 00. It therefore suffices to check the inequality for y∈[0,1/2]y\in[0,1/2].

For y∈[0,1/2]y\in[0,1/2], we have ‖y‖ℤ=y\|y\|_{\mathbb{Z}}=y, and therefore the desired inequality simplifies to

1−20​y2≤cos⁡(2​π​y)≤1−2​y2.1-20y^{2}\leq\cos(2\pi y)\leq 1-2y^{2}.

By Taylor’s theorem (with the Lagrange form of the remainder), for any y∈[0,1/2]y\in[0,1/2], we have

cos⁡(2​π​y)=1−(2​π)22​y2+(2​π)3​sin⁡(2​π​ξ)6​y3\cos(2\pi y)=1-\frac{(2\pi)^{2}}{2}y^{2}+\frac{(2\pi)^{3}\sin(2\pi\xi)}{6}y^{3}

for some ξ∈[0,y]⊆[0,1/2]\xi\in[0,y]\subseteq[0,1/2]. Since sin⁡(2​π​ξ)≥0\sin(2\pi\xi)\geq 0 and y∈[0,1/2]y\in[0,1/2], we can conclude

cos⁡(2​π​y)≥1−(2​π)22​y2=1−(2​π2)​y2≥1−20​y2.\cos(2\pi y)\geq 1-\frac{(2\pi)^{2}}{2}y^{2}=1-(2\pi^{2})y^{2}\geq 1-20y^{2}.

Similarly, we have

cos⁡(2​π​y)=1−(2​π)22​y2+(2​π)4​cos⁡(2​π​ξ)24​y4,\cos(2\pi y)=1-\frac{(2\pi)^{2}}{2}y^{2}+\frac{(2\pi)^{4}\cos(2\pi\xi)}{24}y^{4},

for some ξ∈[0,y]\xi\in[0,y]. Using that cos⁡(2​π​ξ)≤1\cos(2\pi\xi)\leq 1 and y∈[0,1/2]y\in[0,1/2], we have

cos⁡(2​π​y)≤1−(2​π)22​y2+(2​π)424⋅(12)2​y2≤1−2​y2.∎\cos(2\pi y)\leq 1-\frac{(2\pi)^{2}}{2}y^{2}+\frac{(2\pi)^{4}}{24}\cdot\Big(\frac{1}{2}\Big)^{2}y^{2}\leq 1-2y^{2}.\qed

For a prime pp, and y∈ℤy\in\mathbb{Z}, we furthermore define ‖y‖p:=‖y/p‖ℤ=minz∈ℤ⁡|y/p−z|\|y\|_{p}:=\|y/p\|_{\mathbb{Z}}=\min_{z\in\mathbb{Z}}|y/p-z|. Noting that ‖y‖p\|y\|_{p} is pp-periodic, this allows us to define ‖x‖p\|x\|_{p} for any x∈ℤpx\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} by setting ‖x‖p:=‖y‖p\|x\|_{p}:=\|y\|_{p} for any representative y∈ℤy\in\mathbb{Z} of the residue class x∈ℤpx\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}.

Fact 2.3.

For a prime pp, and x1,…,xk∈ℤpx_{1},\dots,x_{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we have

‖x1+⋯+xk‖p2≤k⋅(‖x1‖p2+⋯+‖xk‖p2).\|x_{1}+\dots+x_{k}\|_{p}^{2}\leq k\cdot(\|x_{1}\|_{p}^{2}+\dots+\|x_{k}\|_{p}^{2}).
Proof.

Choosing representatives y1,…,yk∈ℤy_{1},\dots,y_{k}\in\mathbb{Z} for x1,…,xk∈ℤpx_{1},\dots,x_{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, it follows from Fact 2.3 that

‖x1+⋯+xk‖p2=‖(y1/p)+⋯+(yk/p)‖ℤ2≤k⋅(‖y1/p‖ℤ2+⋯+‖yk/p‖ℤ2)=k⋅(‖x1‖p2+⋯+‖xk‖p2).∎\|x_{1}+\dots+x_{k}\|_{p}^{2}=\|(y_{1}/p)+\dots+(y_{k}/p)\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}\leq k\cdot(\|y_{1}/p\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}+\dots+\|y_{k}/p\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2})=k\cdot(\|x_{1}\|_{p}^{2}+\dots+\|x_{k}\|_{p}^{2}).\qed

Finally, we record an easy consequence of the Cauchy-Davenport theorem.

Fact 2.4.

For a prime pp, a subset A⊆ℤpA\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}, and a positive integer kk, let us consider the kk-fold sumset kA=A+⋯+A={a1+⋯+ak:a1,…,ak∈A}kA=A+\dots+A=\{a_{1}+\dots+a_{k}:a_{1},\dots,a_{k}\in A\}. If k​A≠ℤpkA\neq\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we have

|k​A|≥1+k⋅(|A|−1).|kA|\geq 1+k\cdot(|A|-1).
Proof.

Recall that the Cauchy-Davenport theorem states that for any subsets A,B⊆ℤpA,B\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p} with A+B≠ℤpA+B\neq\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we have |A+B|≥|A|+|B|−1|A+B|\geq|A|+|B|-1, and hence |A+B|−1≥(|A|−1)+(|B|−1)|A+B|-1\geq(|A|-1)+(|B|-1). Applying this repeatedly, for any subsets A1,…,AkA_{1},\dots,A_{k} with A1+⋯+Ak≠ℤpA_{1}+\dots+A_{k}\neq\mathbb{Z}_{p} (and hence in particular A1+⋯+Aj≠ℤpA_{1}+\dots+A_{j}\neq\mathbb{Z}_{p} for j=1,…,kj=1,\dots,k) we can conclude

|A1+⋯+Ak|−1≥(|A1+⋯+Ak−1|−1)+(|Ak|−1)≥⋯≥(|A1|−1)+⋯+(|Ak|−1)|A_{1}+\dots+A_{k}|-1\geq(|A_{1}+\dots+A_{k-1}|-1)+(|A_{k}|-1)\geq\dots\geq(|A_{1}|-1)+\dots+(|A_{k}|-1)

Taking A1=⋯=Ak=AA_{1}=\dots=A_{k}=A yields |k​A|−1≥k⋅(|A|−1)|kA|-1\geq k\cdot(|A|-1), which implies the desired inequality. ∎

Finally, for a prime pp and y∈ℤy\in\mathbb{Z}, we define ep​(y)=exp⁡(2​π​i​y/p)e_{p}(y)=\exp(2\pi iy/p). Noting that this function is pp-periodic, we can now defined ep​(x)e_{p}(x) for any x∈ℤpx\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} by setting ep​(x)=ep​(y)=exp⁡(2​π​i​y/p)e_{p}(x)=e_{p}(y)=\exp(2\pi iy/p) for any representative y∈ℤy\in\mathbb{Z} of the residue class x∈ℤpx\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}.

Fact 2.5.

For a prime pp, and x∈ℤpx\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we have

Re⁡(ep​(x))≤1−2​‖x‖p2.\operatorname{Re}(e_{p}(x))\leq 1-2\|x\|_{p}^{2}.
Proof.

Letting y∈ℤy\in\mathbb{Z} be a representative of the residue class x∈ℤpx\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, by Fact 2.2 we have

Re⁡(ep​(x))=Re⁡(ep​(y))=Re⁡(exp⁡(2​π​i​y/p))=cos⁡(2​π​y/p)≤1−2​‖y/p‖ℤ2=1−2​‖y‖p2=1−2​‖x‖p2.∎\operatorname{Re}(e_{p}(x))=\operatorname{Re}(e_{p}(y))=\operatorname{Re}(\exp(2\pi iy/p))=\cos(2\pi y/p)\leq 1-2\|y/p\|_{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}=1-2\|y\|_{p}^{2}=1-2\|x\|_{p}^{2}.\qed

3 Anticoncentration on boolean slices via Fourier Analysis

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.2, taking C=224C=2^{24}. So let pp be a prime, and S⊆ℤpS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p} a subset of size |S|≥2|S|\geq 2. Furthermore, let mm be a positive integers with 224​log⁡|S|=C​log⁡|S|≤m≤10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|2^{24}\log|S|=C\log|S|\leq m\leq 10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|. Note that this in particular implies |S|≥m≥224≥107|S|\geq m\geq 2^{24}\geq 10^{7}.

Let ℤp^\widehat{\mathbb{Z}_{p}} denote the set of Fourier characters over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} (recall that these are the group homomorphisms χ:ℤp→{z∈ℂ:|z|=1}\chi:\mathbb{Z}_{p}\to\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|=1\}). Also recall that we can identify a character χ:ℤp→{z∈ℂ:|z|=1}\chi:\mathbb{Z}_{p}\to\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|=1\} with an element χ∈ℤp\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} via

χ​(x)=ep​(χ​x)\chi(x)=e_{p}(\chi x)

(recall that in Section 2, for any x∈ℤpx\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} we defined ep​(x)=exp⁡(2​π​i​y/p)e_{p}(x)=\exp(2\pi iy/p) where y∈ℤy\in\mathbb{Z} is a representative of the residue class x∈ℤpx\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}).

Given the set S⊆ℤpS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}, in the statement of Theorem 1.2 we consider a uniformly random subset R⊆SR\subseteq S of size mm. We can sample such a uniformly random size-mm subset in the following way, which will be helpful in our proof. We first randomly partition the elements of SS into mm sets S1,…,SmS_{1},\dots,S_{m} with |S1|≥|S2|≥⋯≥|Sm|≥|Sm|−1|S_{1}|\geq|S_{2}|\geq\dots\geq|S_{m}|\geq|S_{m}|-1 (this means that S1,…,SmS_{1},\dots,S_{m} each have size ⌊|S|/m⌋+1\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor+1 or ⌊|S|/m⌋\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor, and exactly the first |S|−m​⌊|S|/m⌋|S|-m\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor of the sets S1,…,SmS_{1},\dots,S_{m} have size ⌈|S|/m⌉+1\lceil|S|/m\rceil+1). Since m≤|S|/4m\leq|S|/4, all of the sets S1,…,SmS_{1},\dots,S_{m} have size at least 44. We then independently pick exactly one element XiX_{i} from each set SiS_{i} to form a set R={X1,…,Xm}R=\{X_{1},\dots,X_{m}\}. It is easy to see that RR is distributed precisely as a uniformly random subset of SS of size mm. Also note that Σ⁡(R)=X1+⋯+Xm\Sigma(R)=X_{1}+\dots+X_{m}. We will write 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}) for the mm-tuple of sets in the partition of SS, and X=(X1,…,Xm)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{m}) for the mm-tuple of elements chosen from these sets.

We write ℙ𝒮\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{S}} and 𝔼𝒮\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}} for probabilities and expectations over the randomness of 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}), i.e. over the randomness of the partition S=S1∪⋯∪SmS=S_{1}\cup\dots\cup S_{m}. For a fixed outcome of 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}), we write ℙX\mathbb{P}_{X} and 𝔼X\mathbb{E}_{X} to denote probabilities and expectations over the randomness of X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}), conditional on 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}). Note that conditional on 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}), the elements Xi∈SiX_{i}\in S_{i} are independent uniformly random elements of SiS_{i} for i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m.

Now, we have

ℙ[Σ(R)=z]=𝔼𝒮[ℙX[Σ(R)=z]],\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z]=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}[\mathbb{P}_{X}[\Sigma(R)=z]],

where the probability ℙX[Σ(R)=z]\mathbb{P}_{X}[\Sigma(R)=z] is conditional on 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}), over the randomness of X=(X1,…,Xn)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}).

Let us fix an outcome of 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}). The standard identity

ℙX[Σ(R)=z]=ℙX[X1+⋯+Xm=z]=1p𝔼X[∑χ∈ℤp^χ(X1+⋯+Xm−z)]=1p∑χ∈ℤp^χ(−z)∏i=1m𝔼X[χ(Xi)]\mathbb{P}_{X}[\Sigma(R)=z]=\mathbb{P}_{X}[X_{1}+\dots+X_{m}=z]=\frac{1}{p}\mathbb{E}_{X}\!\Bigg[\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}}\!\chi(X_{1}+\dots+X_{m}-z)\Bigg]\!=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}}\!\chi(-z)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}_{X}[\chi(X_{i})]

gives

ℙX[Σ(R)=z]≤1p∑χ∈ℤp^|χ(−z)∏i=1m𝔼[χ(Xi)]|=1p∑χ∈ℤp^∏i=1m|𝔼X[χ(Xi)]|.\mathbb{P}_{X}[\Sigma(R)=z]\leq\frac{1}{p}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}}\bigg|\chi(-z)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}[\chi(X_{i})]\bigg|=\frac{1}{p}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}}\ \prod_{i=1}^{m}|\mathbb{E}_{X}[\chi(X_{i})]|. (3.1)

For any χ∈ℤp^\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb{Z}_{p}} and any i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m, we have

|𝔼X​[χ⁡(Xi)]|=|1|Si|​∑x∈Siχ⁡(Xi)|=|1|Si|​∑x∈Siep​(χ​x)|=(1|Si|2​∑x∈Siep​(χ​x)⋅∑x∈Siep​(χ​x)¯)1/2|\mathbb{E}_{X}[\chi(X_{i})]|=\Bigg|\frac{1}{|S_{i}|}\sum_{x\in S_{i}}\chi(X_{i})\Bigg|=\Bigg|\frac{1}{|S_{i}|}\sum_{x\in S_{i}}e_{p}(\chi x)\Bigg|=\Bigg(\frac{1}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\sum_{x\in S_{i}}e_{p}(\chi x)\cdot\overline{\sum_{x\in S_{i}}e_{p}(\chi x)}\Bigg)^{1/2}

As ∑x∈Siep​(χ​x)⋅∑x∈Siep​(χ​x)¯∈ℝ\sum_{x\in S_{i}}e_{p}(\chi x)\cdot\overline{\sum_{x\in S_{i}}e_{p}(\chi x)}\in\mathbb{R} and ep​(χ​x)¯=ep​(−χ​x)\overline{e_{p}(\chi x)}=e_{p}(-\chi x) for all x∈ℤpx\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we can observe that

1|Si|2​∑x∈Siep​(χ​x)⋅∑x∈Siep​(χ​x)¯\displaystyle\frac{1}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\sum_{x\in S_{i}}e_{p}(\chi x)\cdot\overline{\sum_{x\in S_{i}}e_{p}(\chi x)} =1|Si|2​Re⁡(∑x∈Siep​(χ​x)⋅∑x∈Siep​(χ​x)¯)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\operatorname{Re}\Bigg(\sum_{x\in S_{i}}e_{p}(\chi x)\cdot\sum_{x\in S_{i}}\overline{e_{p}(\chi x)}\Bigg)
=1|Si|2​Re⁡(∑x,x′∈Siep​(χ​x−χ​x′))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\operatorname{Re}\Bigg(\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}e_{p}(\chi x-\chi x^{\prime})\Bigg)
≤1|Si|2​∑x,x′∈Si(1−2​‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}(1-2\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2})
=1−2|Si|2​∑x,x′∈Si‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2,\displaystyle=1-\frac{2}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2},

where the inequality is due to Fact 2.5. This yields

|𝔼X[χ(Xi)]|≤(1−2|Si|2∑x,x′∈Si∥χx−χx′∥p2)1/2≤exp(−1|Si|2∑x,x′∈Si∥χx−χx′∥p2).|\mathbb{E}_{X}[\chi(X_{i})]|\leq\Bigg(1-\frac{2}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}\Bigg)^{1/2}\leq\exp\Bigg(-\frac{1}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}\Bigg).

Thus, we obtain

∏i=1m|𝔼X[χ(Xi)]|≤exp(−∑i=1m1|Si|2∑x,x′∈Si∥χx−χx′∥p2)=exp(−ψ(χ)),\prod_{i=1}^{m}|\mathbb{E}_{X}[\chi(X_{i})]|\leq\exp\Bigg(-\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{1}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}\Bigg)=\exp(-\psi(\chi)), (3.2)

where we define

ψ⁡(χ):=∑i=1m1|Si|2​∑x,x′∈Si‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2\psi(\chi):=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\frac{1}{|S_{i}|^{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}

for any χ∈ℤp\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}.

Note that the value of ψ⁡(χ)\psi(\chi) depends on the outcome of 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}), and that for the trivial character corresponding to the element χ=0∈ℤp\chi=0\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we always have ψ⁡(χ)=0\psi(\chi)=0. Also note that for all χ∈ℤp\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we have

ψ⁡(χ)≥m22​|S|2​∑i=1m∑x,x′∈Si‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2,\psi(\chi)\geq\frac{m^{2}}{2|S|^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}, (3.3)

since for i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m we have |Si|≤⌊|S|/m⌋+1≤2​|S|/m|S_{i}|\leq\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor+1\leq\sqrt{2}|S|/m. Finally, since ‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2≤1\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}\leq 1 for all x,x′∈Sx,x^{\prime}\in S, we always have ψ⁡(χ)≤m\psi(\chi)\leq m.

Now, let

A0:={χ∈ℤp:ψ⁡(χ)∈[0,1)},A_{0}:=\Bigg\{\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}:\psi(\chi)\in[0,1)\Bigg\},

and for any positive integer tt, let

At:={χ∈ℤp:ψ⁡(χ)∈[t,2​t)}.A_{t}:=\Bigg\{\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}:\psi(\chi)\in[t,2t)\Bigg\}.

Then we obtain a partition ℤp=A0∪A1∪A2∪A4∪A8∪⋯∪A2⌊log2⁡m⌋\mathbb{Z}_{p}=A_{0}\cup A_{1}\cup A_{2}\cup A_{4}\cup A_{8}\cup\dots\cup A_{2^{\lfloor\log_{2}m\rfloor}} (noting that At=∅A_{t}=\emptyset for t>mt>m). Furthermore, by (3.1) and (3.2) we have

ℙX[Σ(R)=z]≤1p∑χ∈ℤp^∏i=1m|𝔼X[χ(Xi)]|≤1p∑χ∈ℤpexp(−ψ(χ))≤1p|A0|+1p∑ℓ=0⌊log2⁡m⌋|A2ℓ|exp(−2ℓ).\mathbb{P}_{X}[\Sigma(R)=z]\leq\frac{1}{p}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}}\ \prod_{i=1}^{m}|\mathbb{E}_{X}[\chi(X_{i})]|\leq\frac{1}{p}\sum_{\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\exp(-\psi(\chi))\leq\frac{1}{p}|A_{0}|+\frac{1}{p}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\lfloor\log_{2}m\rfloor}|A_{2^{\ell}}|\exp(-2^{\ell}).

Henceforth, we obtain

ℙ[Σ(R)=z]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z] =𝔼𝒮[ℙX[Σ(R)=z]]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}[\mathbb{P}_{X}[\Sigma(R)=z]]
≤𝔼𝒮​[1p​|A0|+1p​∑ℓ=0⌊log2⁡m⌋|A2ℓ|​exp⁡(−2ℓ)]\displaystyle\leq\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}\Bigg[\frac{1}{p}|A_{0}|+\frac{1}{p}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\lfloor\log_{2}m\rfloor}|A_{2^{\ell}}|\exp(-2^{\ell})\Bigg]
=1p​𝔼𝒮​[|A0|]+1p​∑ℓ=0⌊log2⁡m⌋𝔼𝒮​[|A2ℓ|]⋅exp⁡(−2ℓ).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{p}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}[|A_{0}|]+\frac{1}{p}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\lfloor\log_{2}m\rfloor}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}[|A_{2^{\ell}}|]\cdot\exp(-2^{\ell}). (3.4)

In the remaining part of the section, we will bound 𝔼𝒮​[|At|]\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}[|A_{t}|] for t∈{0,1,2,4,8,…}t\in\{0,1,2,4,8,\dots\}. For χ∈ℤp\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, let us define

Ψ⁡(χ)=m|S|2​∑x,x′∈S‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2.\Psi(\chi)=\frac{m}{|S|^{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}.

For any positive integer tt, let

Bt={χ∈ℤp:Ψ⁡(χ)≤t}.B_{t}=\{\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}:\Psi(\chi)\leq t\}.

Furthermore, let DtD_{t} be the collection of χ∈ℤp∖{0}\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}\setminus\{0\} such that there is some y∈ℤpy\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} with

|{x∈S:‖χ​x−y‖p≤8​t/m}|≥34​|S|\Big|\Big\{x\in S:\|\chi x-y\|_{p}\leq 8\sqrt{t/m}\Big\}\Big|\geq\frac{3}{4}|S|

(in other words, this means that there is some “interval” in ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} of length 16​p​t/m16p\sqrt{t/m} containing at least a (3/4)(3/4)-fraction of the elements of χ​S\chi S).

Note that, for any positive integer tt, the sets BtB_{t} and DtD_{t} do not depend on the outcome of 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}) (they only depend on the given set S⊆ℤpS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}). Our next aim is to relate the sets AtA_{t}, which do depend on the outcome of 𝒮=(S1,…,Sm)\mathcal{S}=(S_{1},\dots,S_{m}), to BtB_{t} and DtD_{t}. More specifically, we will show that any χ∈ℤp\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} with χ∉Dt\chi\not\in D_{t} is contained in AtA_{t} with small probability. Similarly, we will show any χ∈Dt∖B32​t\chi\in D_{t}\setminus B_{32t} is contained in AtA_{t} with small probability. We will then obtain the desired bound for 𝔼𝒮​[|At|]\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{S}}[|A_{t}|] by upper-bounding |B32​t||B_{32t}|.

Lemma 3.1.

Let tt be a positive integer, and let χ∈ℤp∖{0}\chi\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}\setminus\{0\} with χ∉Dt\chi\not\in D_{t}. Then we have

ℙ𝒮[ψ(χ)<2t]≤1|S|9.\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{S}}[\psi(\chi)<2t]\leq\frac{1}{|S|^{9}}.
Proof.

For an element x′∈Sx^{\prime}\in S, let i⁡(x′)∈{1,…,m}i(x^{\prime})\in\{1,\dots,m\} denote the index such that x′∈Si⁡(x′)x^{\prime}\in S_{i(x^{\prime})}, i.e. the index of the part of the random partition S=S1∪⋯∪SmS=S_{1}\cup\dots\cup S_{m} containing x′x^{\prime}. Since χ∉Dt\chi\not\in D_{t}, for every fixed x′∈Sx^{\prime}\in S we have |{x∈S:‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p>8​t/m}|≥|S|/4|\{x\in S:\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}>8\sqrt{t/m}\}|\geq|S|/4. Note that, when conditioning on i⁡(x′)i(x^{\prime}) (i.e. exposing and conditioning on which part of the random partition the element x′x^{\prime} belongs to), the set Si⁡(x′)∖{x′}S_{i(x^{\prime})}\setminus\{x^{\prime}\} is a uniformly random subset of S∖{x′}S\setminus\{x^{\prime}\} of size either ⌊|S|/m⌋\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor (if i⁡(x′)≤|S|−m⁡⌊|S|/m⌋i(x^{\prime})\leq|S|-m\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor) or ⌊|S|/m⌋−1\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor-1 (if i⁡(x′)>|S|−m⁡⌊|S|/m⌋i(x^{\prime})>|S|-m\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor). Thus, conditioning on i⁡(x′)i(x^{\prime}), the set Si⁡(x′)∖{x′}S_{i(x^{\prime})}\setminus\{x^{\prime}\} is a uniformly random subset of S∖{x′}S\setminus\{x^{\prime}\} of some given size k≥|S|/(2​m)k\geq|S|/(2m). Recalling that there are at least |S|/4|S|/4 elements x∈S∖{x′}x\in S\setminus\{x^{\prime}\} with ‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p>8​t/m\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}>8\sqrt{t/m}, by the Chernoff bound for hypergeometric distributions (see [8, Theorem 2.10 and Eq. (2.6)]), with probability at least 1−e−k/32≥1−e−|S|/(64m)1-e^{-k/32}\geq 1-e^{-|S|/(64m)} there are at least k/8≥|S|/(16​m)k/8\geq|S|/(16m) different elements x∈Si⁡(x′)∖{x′}x\in S_{i(x^{\prime})}\setminus\{x^{\prime}\} with ‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p>8​t/m\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}>8\sqrt{t/m}.

Thus, by a union bound, with probability at least 1−|S|e−|S|/(64m)1-|S|e^{-|S|/(64m)} for all x′∈Sx^{\prime}\in S we have at least |S|/(16​m)|S|/(16m) different elements x∈Si⁡(x′)∖{x′}x\in S_{i(x^{\prime})}\setminus\{x^{\prime}\} with ‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p>8​t/m\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}>8\sqrt{t/m}. Whenever this happens, by (3.3) we obtain

ψ⁡(χ)≥m22​|S|2​∑i=1m∑x,x′∈Si‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2=m22​|S|2​∑x′∈S∑x∈Si⁡(x′)‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2≥m22​|S|2⋅|S|⋅|S|16​m⋅(8​t/m)2=2​t.\psi(\chi)\geq\frac{m^{2}}{2|S|^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}=\frac{m^{2}}{2|S|^{2}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in S}\sum_{x\in S_{i(x^{\prime})}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}\geq\frac{m^{2}}{2|S|^{2}}\cdot|S|\cdot\frac{|S|}{16m}\cdot\big(8\sqrt{t/m}\big)^{2}=2t.

Thus, we can conclude

ℙ𝒮[ψ(χ)<2t]≤|S|⋅e−|S|/(64m)≤|S|⋅e−10​log⁡|S|=1|S|9,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{S}}[\psi(\chi)<2t]\leq|S|\cdot e^{-|S|/(64m)}\leq|S|\cdot e^{-10\log|S|}=\frac{1}{|S|^{9}},

recalling our assumption m≤10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|m\leq 10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|. ∎

Our next goal is to show that any χ∈Dt∖B32​t\chi\in D_{t}\setminus B_{32t} is contained in AtA_{t} with small probability. For any positive integer tt, and any χ∈Dt\chi\in D_{t}, let yχ∈ℤpy_{\chi}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} be such that |{x∈S:‖χ​x−yχ‖p≤8​t/m}|≥34​|S||\{x\in S:\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}\leq 8\sqrt{t/m}\}|\geq\frac{3}{4}|S| holds, i.e. such that at least a (3/4)(3/4)-fraction of the elements of χ​S\chi S are contained in the “interval” in ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} of length 16​p​t/m16p\sqrt{t/m} around yχy_{\chi}. Note that we can choose yχy_{\chi} to be independent of tt by considering the smallest positive integer tt with χ∈Dt\chi\in D_{t} (choosing a valid yχ∈ℤpy_{\chi}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p} for this smallest value of tt will automatically give a valid yχy_{\chi} for all larger values of tt). Now, let

Jχ,t={x∈ℤp:‖χ​x−yχ‖p≤16​t/m}.J_{\chi,t}=\{x\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}:\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}\leq 16\sqrt{t/m}\}.
Lemma 3.2.

For any positive integer tt, and any χ∈Dt∖B2000​t\chi\in D_{t}\setminus B_{2000t}, we have

∑x∈S∖Jχ,t‖χ​x−yχ‖p2≥200​tm⋅|S|.\sum_{x\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t}}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}\geq\frac{200t}{m}\cdot|S|.
Proof.

By Fact 2.3 we have

‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2≤2​‖χ​x−yχ‖p2+2​‖χ​x′−yχ‖p2,\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}\leq 2\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}+2\|\chi x^{\prime}-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2},

from which we obtain (recalling that χ∉B2000​t\chi\not\in B_{2000t} and hence Ψ⁡(χ)≥2000​t\Psi(\chi)\geq 2000t)

2000​tm≤Ψ⁡(χ)m=1|S|2​∑x,x′∈S‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2≤2|S|2​∑x,x′∈S(‖χ​x−yχ‖p2+‖χ​x′−yχ‖p2)=4|S|​∑x∈S‖χ​x−yχ‖p2.\frac{2000t}{m}\leq\frac{\Psi(\chi)}{m}=\frac{1}{|S|^{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}\leq\frac{2}{|S|^{2}}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S}(\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}+\|\chi x^{\prime}-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2})=\frac{4}{|S|}\sum_{x\in S}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}.

Noting that

∑x∈S‖χ​x−yχ‖p2=∑x∈S∖Jχ,t‖χ​x−yχ‖p2+∑x∈S∩Jχ,t‖χ​x−yχ‖p2≤∑x∈S∖Jχ,t‖χ​x−yχ‖p2+|S∩Jχ,t|⋅265​tm,\sum_{x\in S}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}=\sum_{x\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t}}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}+\sum_{x\in S\cap J_{\chi,t}}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}\leq\sum_{x\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t}}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}+|S\cap J_{\chi,t}|\cdot\frac{265t}{m},

we can conclude that

2000​tm≤4|S|​∑x∈S∖Jχ,t‖χ​x−yχ‖p2+4​|S∩Jχ,t||S|⋅265​tm≤4|S|​∑x∈S∖Jχ,t‖χ​x−yχ‖p2+1024​tm.\frac{2000t}{m}\leq\frac{4}{|S|}\sum_{x\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t}}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}+\frac{4|S\cap J_{\chi,t}|}{|S|}\cdot\frac{265t}{m}\leq\frac{4}{|S|}\sum_{x\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t}}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}+\frac{1024t}{m}.

Thus, we obtain

∑x∈S∖Jχ,t‖χ​x−yχ‖p2≥|S|4⋅976​tm≥200​tm⋅|S|.∎\sum_{x\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t}}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}\geq\frac{|S|}{4}\cdot\frac{976t}{m}\geq\frac{200t}{m}\cdot|S|.\qed
Lemma 3.3.

For any positive integer tt, and any χ∈Dt∖B2000​t\chi\in D_{t}\setminus B_{2000t}, we have

ℙ𝒮[ψ(χ)<2t]≤1|S|9.\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{S}}[\psi(\chi)<2t]\leq\frac{1}{|S|^{9}}.
Proof.

For an element x∈Sx\in S, let us again write i⁡(x)∈{1,…,m}i(x)\in\{1,\dots,m\} for the index such that x∈Si⁡(x)x\in S_{i(x)}. Recall that |{x′∈S:‖χ​x′−yχ‖p≤8​t/m}|≥34​|S||\{x^{\prime}\in S:\|\chi x^{\prime}-y_{\chi}\|_{p}\leq 8\sqrt{t/m}\}|\geq\frac{3}{4}|S|, so at least 3​|S|/43|S|/4 elements x′∈Sx^{\prime}\in S satisfy ‖χ​x′−yχ‖p≤8​t/m\|\chi x^{\prime}-y_{\chi}\|_{p}\leq 8\sqrt{t/m}.

Now, for any fixed x∈S∖Jχ,tx\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t} (i.e. any x∈Sx\in S with ‖χ​x−yχ‖p>16​t/m\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}>16\sqrt{t/m}), when conditioning on i⁡(x)i(x), the set Si⁡(x)∖{x}S_{i(x)}\setminus\{x\} is a uniformly random subset of S∖{x}S\setminus\{x\} of size either ⌊|S|/m⌋\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor (if i⁡(x)≤|S|−m⁡⌊|S|/m⌋i(x)\leq|S|-m\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor) or ⌊|S|/m⌋−1\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor-1 (if i⁡(x)>|S|−m⁡⌊|S|/m⌋i(x)>|S|-m\lfloor|S|/m\rfloor). Thus, conditioning on i⁡(x)i(x), the set Si⁡(x)∖{x}S_{i(x)}\setminus\{x\} is a uniformly random subset of S∖{x}S\setminus\{x\} of some given size k≥|S|/(2​m)k\geq|S|/(2m). Recalling that there are at least 3​|S|/43|S|/4 elements x′∈S∖{x}x^{\prime}\in S\setminus\{x\} with ‖χ​x′−yχ‖p≤8​t/m\|\chi x^{\prime}-y_{\chi}\|_{p}\leq 8\sqrt{t/m}, by the Chernoff bound for hypergeometric distributions (see [8, Theorem 2.10 and Eq. (2.6)]), with probability at least 1−e−k/24≥1−e−|S|/(48m)1-e^{-k/24}\geq 1-e^{-|S|/(48m)} there are at least k/2≥|S|/(4​m)k/2\geq|S|/(4m) different elements x′∈Si⁡(x)∖{x}x^{\prime}\in S_{i(x)}\setminus\{x\} with ‖χ​x′−yχ‖p≤8​t/m≤‖χ​x−yχ‖p/2\|\chi x^{\prime}-y_{\chi}\|_{p}\leq 8\sqrt{t/m}\leq\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}/2. These elements x′∈Si⁡(x)∖{x}x^{\prime}\in S_{i(x)}\setminus\{x\} then satisfy ‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p≥‖χ​x−yχ‖p−‖χ​x′−yχ‖p≥‖χ​x−yχ‖p/2\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}\geq\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}-\|\chi x^{\prime}-y_{\chi}\|_{p}\geq\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}/2

Thus, by a union bound, with probability at least 1−|S|e−|S|/(48m)1-|S|e^{-|S|/(48m)} for all x∈S∖Jχ,tx\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t} we have at least |S|/(4​m)|S|/(4m) different elements x′∈Si⁡(x)∖{x}x^{\prime}\in S_{i(x)}\setminus\{x\} with ‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p≥‖χ​x−yχ‖p/2\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}\geq\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}/2. Whenever this happens, by (3.3) we obtain

ψ⁡(χ)\displaystyle\psi(\chi) ≥m22​|S|2​∑i=1m∑x,x′∈Si‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2\displaystyle\geq\frac{m^{2}}{2|S|^{2}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{x,x^{\prime}\in S_{i}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}
=m22​|S|2⋅∑x∈S∑x′∈Si⁡(x)‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2\displaystyle=\frac{m^{2}}{2|S|^{2}}\cdot\sum_{x\in S}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in S_{i(x)}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}
≥m22​|S|2⋅∑x∈S∖Jχ,t∑x′∈Si⁡(x)‖χ​x−χ​x′‖p2\displaystyle\geq\frac{m^{2}}{2|S|^{2}}\cdot\sum_{x\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t}}\sum_{x^{\prime}\in S_{i(x)}}\|\chi x-\chi x^{\prime}\|_{p}^{2}
≥m22​|S|2⋅∑x∈S∖Jχ,t|S|4​m⋅(‖χ​x−yχ‖p/2)2\displaystyle\geq\frac{m^{2}}{2|S|^{2}}\cdot\sum_{x\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t}}\frac{|S|}{4m}\cdot(\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}/2)^{2}
=m32​|S|⋅∑x∈S∖Jχ,t‖χ​x−yχ‖p2≥m32​|S|⋅200​tm⋅|S|≥5​t,\displaystyle=\frac{m}{32|S|}\cdot\sum_{x\in S\setminus J_{\chi,t}}\|\chi x-y_{\chi}\|_{p}^{2}\geq\frac{m}{32|S|}\cdot\frac{200t}{m}\cdot|S|\geq 5t,

where for the penultimate inequality we used Lemma 3.2. Thus, we can conclude

ℙ𝒮[ψ(χ)<2t]≤ℙ𝒮[ψ(χ)<5t]≤|S|⋅e−|S|/(48m)≤|S|⋅e−10​log⁡|S|=1|S|9,\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{S}}[\psi(\chi)<2t]\leq\mathbb{P}_{\mathcal{S}}[\psi(\chi)<5t]\leq|S|\cdot e^{-|S|/(48m)}\leq|S|\cdot e^{-10\log|S|}=\frac{1}{|S|^{9}},

recalling our assumption m≤10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|m\leq 10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|. ∎

Our final ingredient for the proof of Theorem 1.3 is the following upper bound for |Bt||B_{t}|.

Lemma 3.4.

For any positive integer t≤m/2000t\leq m/2000, we have

|Bt|≤1+200​p​t|S|​m.|B_{t}|\leq 1+\frac{200p\sqrt{t}}{|S|\sqrt{m}}.

We will need some auxiliary lemmas for the proof of Lemma 3.4. For δ>0\delta>0, define

Lemma 3.5.

4 Combinatorial anticoncentration deductions

In this section, we use combinatorial arguments to deduce Corollary 1.4 from Theorem 1.3, and to also derive another corollary that we will need in our proof of Theorem 1.2.

We start with the following simple observation.

Lemma 4.1.

Let pp be a prime, let S⊆ℤpS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}, and let m≤|S|m\leq|S| be a positive integer. Now, let R⊆SR\subseteq S be a uniformly random subset of SS of size mm. Then we have

maxzℙ[Σ(R)=z]≤1|S|−m+1,\max_{z}\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z]\leq\frac{1}{|S|-m+1},
Proof.

We sample the uniformly random subset R⊆SR\subseteq S of size RR by first sampling a uniformly random subset R′⊆SR^{\prime}\subseteq S of size m−1m-1, and then sampling a uniformly random element r∈S∖R′r\in S\setminus R^{\prime}, setting R=R′∪{r}R=R^{\prime}\cup\{r\}.

Conditional on any outcome of R′R^{\prime}, for any z∈ℤpz\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we have

ℙ⁡[Σ⁡(R)=z∣R′]=ℙ⁡[r=z−Σ⁡(R′)∣R′]≤1|S∖R′|=1|S|−m+1.\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z\mid R^{\prime}]=\mathbb{P}[r=z-\Sigma(R^{\prime})\mid R^{\prime}]\leq\frac{1}{|S\setminus R^{\prime}|}=\frac{1}{|S|-m+1}.

Thus, for any z∈ℤpz\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we can conclude

ℙ[Σ(R)=z]≤1|S|−m+1.∎\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z]\leq\frac{1}{|S|-m+1}.\qed

Now, we are ready to deduce Corollary 1.4 from Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 1.3.

Proof of Corollary 1.4.

Let the constant C>0C>0 be as in Theorem 1.2. We may assume that |S||S| is sufficiently large with respect to ε\varepsilon, since the statement in Corollary 1.4 trivially holds for small |S||S| (by choosing a large constant Cε′>0C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}>0). In particular, we may assume |S|≥(4000​C/ε)⋅(log⁡|S|)2|S|\geq(4000C/\varepsilon)\cdot(\log|S|)^{2} (and |S|≥10|S|\geq 10).

If m≤C​log⁡|S|m\leq C\log|S|, the assertion of Corollary 1.4 follows directly from Lemma 4.1, since then (noting that m≤C​log⁡|S|≤|S|/2m\leq C\log|S|\leq|S|/2)

maxzℙ[Σ(R)=z]≤1|S|−m+1≤1|S|/2≤2​C​log⁡|S||S|​m≤1p+2​C⋅log⁡|S||S|​m.\max_{z}\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z]\leq\frac{1}{|S|-m+1}\leq\frac{1}{|S|/2}\leq\frac{2\sqrt{C\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m}}\leq\frac{1}{p}+\frac{2\sqrt{C}\cdot\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m}}.

Furthermore, if C​log⁡|S|≤m≤10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|C\log|S|\leq m\leq 10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|, the assertion of Corollary 1.4 follows directly from Theorem 1.3. We may therefore assume that m≥10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|m\geq 10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|.

Let m2=⌊ε​10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|⌋≥(ε/2)​10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|m_{2}=\lfloor\varepsilon 10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|\rfloor\geq(\varepsilon/2)10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|, and note that m2≤mm_{2}\leq m. Letting m1=m−m2m_{1}=m-m_{2}, we may now sample the uniformly random subset R⊆SR\subseteq S of size mm by first sampling a uniformly random subset R1⊆SR_{1}\subseteq S of size m1m_{1}, and then sampling a uniformly random subset R2⊆S∖R1R_{2}\subseteq S\setminus R_{1} of size m2m_{2}, setting R=R1∪R2R=R_{1}\cup R_{2} (then RR has size m1+m2=mm_{1}+m_{2}=m).

Note for any outcome of R1R_{1}, we have |S∖R1|≥|S|−m≥|S|−(1−ε)|S|=ε​|S||S\setminus R_{1}|\geq|S|-m\geq|S|-(1-\varepsilon)|S|=\varepsilon|S| and hence m2≤ε​10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|≤10−3​|S∖R1|/log⁡|S∖R1|m_{2}\leq\varepsilon 10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|\leq 10^{-3}|S\setminus R_{1}|/\log|S\setminus R_{1}|, as well as m2≥(ε/2)​10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|≥C​log⁡|S|≥C​log⁡|S∖R1|m_{2}\geq(\varepsilon/2)10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|\geq C\log|S|\geq C\log|S\setminus R_{1}|. Therefore, conditional on any outcome of R1R_{1}, by Theorem 1.3, for any z∈ℤpz\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we have

ℙ⁡[Σ⁡(R)=z∣R1]=ℙ⁡[Σ⁡(R2)=z−Σ⁡(R1)∣R1]≤1p+C|S∖R1|​m2.\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z\mid R_{1}]=\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R_{2})=z-\Sigma(R_{1})\mid R_{1}]\leq\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C}{|S\setminus R_{1}|\sqrt{m_{2}}}.

Noting that |S∖R1|​m2≥ε​|S|⋅(ε/2)​10−3​|S|/log⁡|S|≥ε3/2​|S|3/2/(50​log⁡|S|)|S\setminus R_{1}|\sqrt{m_{2}}\geq\varepsilon|S|\cdot\sqrt{(\varepsilon/2)10^{-3}|S|/\log|S|}\geq\varepsilon^{3/2}|S|^{3/2}/(50\sqrt{\log|S|}), we can conclude that

ℙ⁡[Σ⁡(R)=z∣R1]≤1p+50Cε−3/2log⁡|S||S|3/2≤1p+50Cε−3/2log⁡|S||S|​m\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z\mid R_{1}]\leq\frac{1}{p}+\frac{50C\varepsilon^{-3/2}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{3/2}}\leq\frac{1}{p}+\frac{50C\varepsilon^{-3/2}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m}}

for any outcome of R1R_{1} and any z∈ℤpz\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}. This shows that

ℙ[Σ(R)=z]≤1p+50Cε−3/2log⁡|S||S|​m\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R)=z]\leq\frac{1}{p}+\frac{50C\varepsilon^{-3/2}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m}}

for any z∈ℤpz\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, finishing the proof. ∎

In the proof of our main result in Theorem 1.2, we will use the following corollary of Corollary 1.4 several times. Rather than with a single random subset R⊆SR\subseteq S of a given size, this corollary is concerned with a uniformly random chain of subsets R1⊆R1⊆⋯⊆Rk⊆SR_{1}\subseteq R_{1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq R_{k}\subseteq S of given sizes.

Corollary 4.2.

For every positive integer kk, there exists a constant Ck>0C_{k}>0 such that the following holds. Let pp be a prime, let S⊆ℤpS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p} be a subset of size |S|≥2|S|\geq 2, and consider integers 1≤m1<⋯<mk<|S|1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{k}<|S|. Now, let R1⊆⋯⊆Rk⊆SR_{1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq R_{k}\subseteq S be a uniformly random chain of subsets of SS satisfying |Ri|=mi|R_{i}|=m_{i} for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k. Then for any z1,…,zk∈ℤpz_{1},\dots,z_{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}, we have

ℙ[Σ(Ri)=zi for i=1,…,k]≤∑j=0k∏i∈{0,…,k}∖{j}(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi),\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R_{i})=z_{i}\text{ for }i=1,\dots,k]\leq\sum_{j=0}^{k}\,\prod_{i\in\{0,\dots,k\}\setminus\{j\}}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg),

where we set m0=0m_{0}=0 and mk+1=|S|m_{k+1}=|S|.

Proof.

Let ε=1/(k+1)\varepsilon=1/(k+1), and let us define Ck=Cε′/εC_{k}=C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon for the constant Cε′C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon} in Corollary 1.4. Also let z1,…,zk∈ℤpz_{1},\dots,z_{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}.

As (m1−m0)+(m2−m1)+⋯+(mk+1−mk)=mk+1−m0=|S|(m_{1}-m_{0})+(m_{2}-m_{1})+\dots+(m_{k+1}-m_{k})=m_{k+1}-m_{0}=|S|, we can fix an index j∈{0,…,k}j\in\{0,\dots,k\} with mj+1−mj≥|S|/(k+1)m_{j+1}-m_{j}\geq|S|/(k+1). It now suffices to prove

ℙ[Σ(Ri)=zi for i=1,…,k]≤∏i∈{0,…,k}∖{j}(1p+(Cε′/ε)​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi).\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R_{i})=z_{i}\text{ for }i=1,\dots,k]\leq\prod_{i\in\{0,\dots,k\}\setminus\{j\}}\,\,\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{(C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon)\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg).

For i=j+1,…,ki=j+1,\dots,k, let Ri′=S∖RiR^{\prime}_{i}=S\setminus R_{i}, and note that then we have Rk′⊆Rk−1′⊆⋯⊆Rj+1′⊆S∖RjR^{\prime}_{k}\subseteq R^{\prime}_{k-1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq R^{\prime}_{j+1}\subseteq S\setminus R_{j} and |Ri′|=|S|−mi|R^{\prime}_{i}|=|S|-m_{i} for i=j+1,…,ki=j+1,\dots,k. Furthermore, conditional on any outcome of R1,…,RjR_{1},\dots,R_{j}, the chain of sets Rk′⊆Rk−1′⊆⋯⊆Rj+1′⊆S∖RjR^{\prime}_{k}\subseteq R^{\prime}_{k-1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq R^{\prime}_{j+1}\subseteq S\setminus R_{j} is uniformly random among all such nested chains in S∖RjS\setminus R_{j} with the appropriate sizes |Ri′|=|S|−mi|R^{\prime}_{i}|=|S|-m_{i} for i=j+1,…,ki=j+1,\dots,k.

We expose the random chain R1⊆R1⊆⋯⊆Rk⊆SR_{1}\subseteq R_{1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq R_{k}\subseteq S by first exposing R1R_{1} (this is a uniformly random subset of SS of size m1m_{1}), then R2∖R1R_{2}\setminus R_{1} (this is now a uniformly random subset of S∖R1S\setminus R_{1} of size m2−m1m_{2}-m_{1}), and so on until we expose Rj∖Rj−1R_{j}\setminus R_{j-1} (which is a uniformly random subset of S∖Rj−1S\setminus R_{j-1} of size mj−mj−1m_{j}-m_{j-1}). At this point we have determined R1,…,RjR_{1},\dots,R_{j}. Now, we expose Rk′R^{\prime}_{k} (this is a uniformly random subset of S∖RjS\setminus R_{j} of size |S|−mk|S|-m_{k}), then Rk−1′∖Rk′R^{\prime}_{k-1}\setminus R^{\prime}_{k} (this is a uniformly random subset of S∖(Rj∪Rk′)S\setminus(R_{j}\cup R^{\prime}_{k}) of size (|S|−mk−1)−(|S|−mk)=mk−mk−1(|S|-m_{k-1})-(|S|-m_{k})=m_{k}-m_{k-1}), and so on until we have exposed the entire chain Rk′⊆Rk−1′⊆⋯⊆Rj+1′R^{\prime}_{k}\subseteq R^{\prime}_{k-1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq R^{\prime}_{j+1} as well. This now determines R1⊆R1⊆⋯⊆RkR_{1}\subseteq R_{1}\subseteq\dots\subseteq R_{k}.

Observe that we have Σ⁡(Ri)=zi\Sigma(R_{i})=z_{i} for i=1,…,ki=1,\dots,k if and only if all of the following conditions hold: Σ⁡(R1)=z1\Sigma(R_{1})=z_{1}, and Σ⁡(Ri∖Ri−1)=zi−zi−1\Sigma(R_{i}\setminus R_{i-1})=z_{i}-z_{i-1} for i=2,…,ji=2,\dots,j, and Σ⁡(Rk′)=Σ⁡(S)−zk\Sigma(R^{\prime}_{k})=\Sigma(S)-z_{k}, and Σ⁡(Ri′∖Ri+1′)=zi+1−zi\Sigma(R^{\prime}_{i}\setminus R^{\prime}_{i+1})=z_{i+1}-z_{i} for i=j+1,…,k−1i=j+1,\dots,k-1. This means that at every step of the exposure procedure above, we choose a uniformly random subset of the not-yet-chosen elements of a certain prescribed size, and we need to bound the probability of attaining a certain sum (conditional on our previously exposed information). At each such step, we can use Corollary 1.4 to bound this probability. For this, we crucially use that at any step we choose at most a (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon)-fraction of the not-yet-chosen elements. Indeed, this holds since at the very end of the procedure mj+1−mj≥|S|/(k+1)=ε​|S|m_{j+1}-m_{j}\geq|S|/(k+1)=\varepsilon|S| elements remain unchosen (namely, the elements in Rj+1∖RjR_{j+1}\setminus R_{j}), and so we cannot reduce the number of leftover elements by a factor smaller than ε\varepsilon at any step. Also note that at any step the set of not-yet-chosen elements has size at least ε​|S|\varepsilon|S|.

Thus, at any step, conditional on the previously exposed information, the probability of our random subset attaining the desired sum can indeed be bounded by Corollary 1.4. More specifically, the probability of having Σ⁡(R1)=z1\Sigma(R_{1})=z_{1} is at most

1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​m1=1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​m1−m0.\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{m_{1}}}=\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{m_{1}-m_{0}}}.

For any i=2,…,ji=2,\dots,j, the probability of having Σ⁡(Ri∖Ri−1)=zi−zi−1\Sigma(R_{i}\setminus R_{i-1})=z_{i}-z_{i-1}, conditional on the previously exposed information, is at most

1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​mi−mi−1.\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{m_{i}-m_{i-1}}}.

The probability of having Σ⁡(Rk′)=Σ⁡(S)−zk\Sigma(R^{\prime}_{k})=\Sigma(S)-z_{k}, conditional on the previously exposed information determining S∖RjS\setminus R_{j}, is at most

1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​|S|−mk=1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​mk+1−mk.\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{|S|-m_{k}}}=\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{m_{k+1}-m_{k}}}.

And, finally, for i=j+1,…,k−1i=j+1,\dots,k-1, the probability of having Σ⁡(Ri′∖Ri+1′)=zi+1−zi\Sigma(R^{\prime}_{i}\setminus R^{\prime}_{i+1})=z_{i+1}-z_{i}, conditional on the previously exposed information, is at most

1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​mi+1−mi.\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}.

Altogether this shows that

ℙ[Σ(Ri)=zi for i=1,…,k]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(R_{i})=z_{i}\text{ for }i=1,\dots,k]
≤(1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​m1−m0)⋅∏i=2j(1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​mi−mi−1)⋅(1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​mk+1−mk)\displaystyle\qquad\leq\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{m_{1}-m_{0}}}\Bigg)\cdot\prod_{i=2}^{j}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{m_{i}-m_{i-1}}}\Bigg)\cdot\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{m_{k+1}-m_{k}}}\Bigg)
⋅∏i=j+1k(1p+Cε′​log⁡|S|ε​|S|​mi+1−mi)\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\cdot\prod_{i=j+1}^{k}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{\varepsilon|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)
=∏i∈{0,…,k}∖{j}(1p+(Cε′/ε)​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi).∎\displaystyle\qquad=\prod_{i\in\{0,\dots,k\}\setminus\{j\}}\,\,\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{(C^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}/\varepsilon)\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg).\qed

We end this section with the following bound for the sum of the terms on the right-hand side of the inequality in Corollary 4.2 obtained for different choices of m1<⋯<mkm_{1}<\dots<m_{k}.

Lemma 4.3.

Let kk be a positive integer, and let Ck>0C_{k}>0 be the constant in Corollary 4.2. Furthermore, let pp be a prime, and let S⊆ℤpS\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p} be a subset of size |S|≥2|S|\geq 2. As in Corollary 4.2, let m0=0m_{0}=0 and mk+1=|S|m_{k+1}=|S|. Then, we have

∑1≤m1<⋯<mk<|S|∑j=0k∏i∈{0,…,k}∖{j}(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)≤(k+1)⋅(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)k,\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{k}<|S|}\,\sum_{j=0}^{k}\,\prod_{i\in\{0,\dots,k\}\setminus\{j\}}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)\leq(k+1)\cdot\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{k},

where the sum on the left-hand side is taken over all kk-tuples (m1,…,mk)∈{1,…,|S|}k(m_{1},\dots,m_{k})\in\{1,\dots,|S|\}^{k} satisfying 1≤m1<⋯<mk<|S|1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{k}<|S|.

Proof.

We first show by induction that for h=0,…,kh=0,\dots,k we have

∑1≤m1<⋯<mh<|S|∏i=0h−1(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)≤(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)h.\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{h}<|S|}\,\prod_{i=0}^{h-1}\,\,\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)\leq\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{h}. (4.1)

For h=0h=0, the sum on the right-hand side of (4.1) is has exactly one term, corresponding to the unique empty 00-tuple, and this term is 11 (as an empty product). Thus, for h=0h=0 the inequality reads 1≤11\leq 1, which is true. So let us now assume that we already showed (4.1) for some h∈{0,…,k−1}h\in\{0,\dots,k-1\}. Now, for h+1h+1, we have

∑1≤m1<⋯<mh+1<|S|∏i=0h(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{h+1}<|S|}\,\prod_{i=0}^{h}\,\,\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)
=∑1≤m1<⋯<mh<|S|(∏i=0h−1(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)⋅∑mh+1=mh+1|S|−1(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mh+1−mh))\displaystyle\qquad\qquad=\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{h}<|S|}\Bigg(\prod_{i=0}^{h-1}\,\,\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)\cdot\sum_{m_{h+1}=m_{h}+1}^{|S|-1}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{h+1}-m_{h}}}\Bigg)\Bigg)
≤∑1≤m1<⋯<mh<|S|(∏i=0h−1(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)⋅(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2))\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\leq\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{h}<|S|}\Bigg(\prod_{i=0}^{h-1}\,\,\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)\cdot\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)\Bigg)
=(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)⋅∑1≤m1<⋯<mh<|S|∏i=0h−1(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)\displaystyle\qquad\qquad=\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)\cdot\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{h}<|S|}\prod_{i=0}^{h-1}\,\,\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)
≤(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)⋅(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)h=(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)h+1,\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\leq\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)\cdot\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{h}=\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{h+1},

where the second inequality holds by the inductive assumption, and the first inequality follows from

∑mh+1=mh+1|S|−1Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mh+1−mh≤∑t=1|S|Ck​log⁡|S||S|​t≤Ck​log⁡|S||S|⋅2​|S|=2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2.\sum_{m_{h+1}=m_{h}+1}^{|S|-1}\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{h+1}-m_{h}}}\leq\sum_{t=1}^{|S|}\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{t}}\leq\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|}\cdot 2\sqrt{|S|}=\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}.

This proves (4.1), as claimed.

Let us now turn to the inequality in the lemma statement. To show this inequality, it clearly suffices to show

∑1≤m1<⋯<mk<|S|∏i∈{0,…,k}∖{j}(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)≤(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)k\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{k}<|S|}\,\prod_{i\in\{0,\dots,k\}\setminus\{j\}}\,\,\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)\leq\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{k}

for all j=0,…,kj=0,\dots,k. So let us fix j∈{0,…,k}j\in\{0,\dots,k\}. Now, we have

∑1≤m1<⋯<mk<|S|∏i∈{0,…,k}∖{j}(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)\displaystyle\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{k}<|S|}\,\prod_{i\in\{0,\dots,k\}\setminus\{j\}}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)
≤∑1≤m1<⋯<mj<|S|∑1≤mj+1<⋯<mk<|S|∏i=0j−1(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)⋅∏i=j+1k(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)\displaystyle\qquad\leq\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{j}<|S|}\,\,\sum_{1\leq m_{j+1}<\dots<m_{k}<|S|}\,\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)\cdot\prod_{i=j+1}^{k}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)
=∑1≤m1<⋯<mj<|S|∏i=0j−1(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)⋅∑1≤mj+1<⋯<mk<|S|∏i=j+1k(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{j}<|S|}\,\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)\cdot\sum_{1\leq m_{j+1}<\dots<m_{k}<|S|}\,\prod_{i=j+1}^{k}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)
=∑1≤m1<⋯<mj<|S|∏i=0j−1(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1−mi)⋅∑1≤m1′<⋯<mk−j′<|S|∏i=0k−j−1(1p+Ck​log⁡|S||S|​mi+1′−mi′)\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{1\leq m_{1}<\dots<m_{j}<|S|}\,\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m_{i+1}-m_{i}}}\Bigg)\cdot\sum_{1\leq m^{\prime}_{1}<\dots<m^{\prime}_{k-j}<|S|}\prod_{i=0}^{k-j-1}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{m^{\prime}_{i+1}-m^{\prime}_{i}}}\Bigg)
≤(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)j⋅(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)k−j=(|S|p+2​Ck​log⁡|S||S|1/2)k,\displaystyle\qquad\leq\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{j}\cdot\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{k-j}=\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{2C_{k}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{k},

5 Rearrangement conjecture

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.2, using Corollary 1.4. Let 0<α<1/20<\alpha<1/2 (note that in Theorem 1.2 we may assume without loss of generality that α<1/2\alpha<1/2, since the statement for some value of α\alpha automatically implies the same statement for all larger values of α\alpha). Let D=⌈3/α⌉D=\lceil 3/\alpha\rceil and let CαC_{\alpha} be large enough such that Cα≥(104⋅240​D)1/αC_{\alpha}\geq(10^{4}\cdot 2^{40D})^{1/\alpha} and Cα≥(D+1)⋅2D⋅D14​D2≥100⋅(5​D)2​D≥(40​D)DC_{\alpha}\geq(D+1)\cdot 2^{D}\cdot D^{14D^{2}}\geq 100\cdot(5D)^{2D}\geq(40D)^{D} and such that we have 4​max⁡(CD,C1)​log⁡n/n1/2≤n−α4\max(C_{D},C_{1})\sqrt{\log n}/n^{1/2}\leq n^{-\alpha} for all n≥Cαn\geq C_{\alpha} (where C1C_{1} and CDC_{D} denote the constants in Corollary 4.2 for k=1k=1 and k=Dk=D).

Now, let S⊆ℤp∖{0}S\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{p}\setminus\{0\} be as in Theorem 1.2, meaning that Cα≤|S|≤p1−αC_{\alpha}\leq|S|\leq p^{1-\alpha}. Then in particular we have |S|/p≤p−α≤|S|−α|S|/p\leq p^{-\alpha}\leq|S|^{-\alpha} as well as 4​C1​log⁡|S|/|S|1/2≤|S|−α4C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}/|S|^{1/2}\leq|S|^{-\alpha} and 4​CD​log⁡|S|/|S|1/2≤|S|−α4C_{D}\sqrt{\log|S|}/|S|^{1/2}\leq|S|^{-\alpha}.

We need to show that there is an ordering s1,s2,…,s|S|s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{|S|} of the elements of SS such that all partial sums s1,s1+s2,…,s1+s2+⋯+s|S|s_{1},s_{1}+s_{2},\dots,s_{1}+s_{2}+\dots+s_{|S|} are distinct. In other words, this means that all the partial sums sa+sa+1+⋯+sbs_{a}+s_{a+1}+\dots+s_{b} must be non-zero in ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} for all 2≤a≤b≤|S|2\leq a\leq b\leq|S|.

An ordering s1,s2,…,s|S|s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{|S|} of the elements of SS corresponds to a bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S, where σ⁡(a)=sa\sigma(a)=s_{a} for all a∈{1,…,|S|}a\in\{1,\dots,|S|\}. For a bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S, we define

Σ⁡(σ,[a,b])=∑i=abσ⁡(i)=σ⁡(a)+σ⁡(a+1)+⋯+σ⁡(b)\Sigma(\sigma,[a,b])=\sum_{i=a}^{b}\sigma(i)=\sigma(a)+\sigma(a+1)+\dots+\sigma(b)

for all 1≤a<b≤|S|1\leq a<b\leq|S|. This is precisely sa+sa+1+⋯+sbs_{a}+s_{a+1}+\dots+s_{b} for the corresponding ordering s1,s2,…,s|S|s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{|S|} of the elements of SS. Thus, to prove Theorem 1.2, our task is to find a bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S such that Σ⁡(σ,[a,b])≠0\Sigma(\sigma,[a,b])\neq 0 for all 2≤a<b≤|S|2\leq a<b\leq|S|.

Our starting point is to consider a uniformly random bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S. Typically, for such a random bijection there will be some (but only few) pairs (a,b)(a,b) with 2≤a<b≤|S|2\leq a<b\leq|S| and Σ⁡(σ,[a,b])=0\Sigma(\sigma,[a,b])=0. Instead of σ\sigma itself, we will therefore consider σ∘π\sigma\circ\pi for a suitable permutation π:{1,…,|S|}→{1,…,|S|}\pi:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to\{1,\dots,|S|\} obtained by composing certain transpositions in order to change Σ⁡(σ,[a,b])\Sigma(\sigma,[a,b]) for those intervals [a,b][a,b] where we have Σ⁡(σ,[a,b])=0\Sigma(\sigma,[a,b])=0.

Given a bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S, let B⁡(σ)⊆{3,…,|S|}B(\sigma)\subseteq\{3,\dots,|S|\} be the set consisting of the right endpoints of all intervals [a,b][a,b] with 2≤a<b≤|S|2\leq a<b\leq|S| and Σ⁡(σ,[a,b])=0\Sigma(\sigma,[a,b])=0. More formally, let B⁡(σ)⊆{1,…,|S|}B(\sigma)\subseteq\{1,\dots,|S|\} be the set of all b∈{1,…,|S|}b\in\{1,\dots,|S|\} such that there exists a∈{2,…,|S|}a\in\{2,\dots,|S|\} with a<ba<b and Σ⁡(σ,[a,b])=0\Sigma(\sigma,[a,b])=0 (note that then automatically b≥3b\geq 3).

We will now consider various bad events (namely the events ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1}, ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} and ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3} defined below), and show via our anticoncentration results in Corollary 4.2 that for a uniformly random bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S these bad events occur with very small probability. In order to prove Theorem 1.2, we can then fix a bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S such that none of these events holds, and take this as a starting point to construct the desired ordering s1,…,s|S|s_{1},\dots,s_{|S|} of the elements in SS.

Lemma 5.1.

For a uniformly random bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S, let ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} be the event that there is some b∈B⁡(σ)b\in B(\sigma) with |S|−30​D≤b≤|S||S|-30D\leq b\leq|S|. Then we have ℙ⁡[ℬ1]≤1/100\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}_{1}]\leq 1/100.

Lemma 5.2.

For a uniformly random bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S, let ℬ2\mathcal{B}_{2} be the event that there exists z∈{1,…,|S|}z\in\{1,\dots,|S|\} with |B⁡(σ)∩{z−10​D,…,z+10​D}|>D|B(\sigma)\cap\{z-10D,\dots,z+10D\}|>D. Then we have ℙ⁡[ℬ2]≤3/100\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}_{2}]\leq 3/100.

We will prove Lemmas 5.1 and 5.2 further below (towards the end of this section). The proofs of these lemmas rely on our anticoncentration results established in the previous sections.

For a permutation π:{1,…,|S|}→{1,…,|S|}\pi:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to\{1,\dots,|S|\}, let Fix⁡(π)={t∈{1,…,|S|}:π⁡(t)=t}\operatorname{Fix}(\pi)=\{t\in\{1,\dots,|S|\}:\pi(t)=t\} denote the set of fixed points of π\pi. For any x,y∈{1,…,|S|}x,y\in\{1,\dots,|S|\} with x<yx<y, let πx,y:{1,…,|S|}→{1,…,|S|}\pi_{x,y}:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to\{1,\dots,|S|\} denote the transposition interchanging xx and yy (i.e. πx,y​(x)=y\pi_{x,y}(x)=y, πx,y​(y)=x\pi_{x,y}(y)=x and πx,y​(t)=t\pi_{x,y}(t)=t for all t∈{1,…,|S|}∖{x,y}t\in\{1,\dots,|S|\}\setminus\{x,y\}).

Let us say that a collection PP of pairs (x,y)(x,y) with x,y∈{1,…,|S|}x,y\in\{1,\dots,|S|\} and x<yx<y is admissible if all the elements of {1,…,|S|}\{1,\dots,|S|\} appearing in the pairs in PP are distinct, and we have y−x≤5​Dy-x\leq 5D for all (x,y)∈P(x,y)\in P. To any such admissible PP, we can associate the bijection πP:{1,…,|S|}→{1,…,|S|}\pi_{P}:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to\{1,\dots,|S|\} obtained by composing the transpositions πx,y\pi_{x,y} for all (x,y)∈P(x,y)\in P (note that here the order of these transpositions does not matter, since they all commute with each other as their supports are disjoint). We say that a permutation π:{1,…,|S|}→{1,…,|S|}\pi:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to\{1,\dots,|S|\} is admissible, if π=πP\pi=\pi_{P} for some admissible PP. Also note that PP can be uniquely reconstructed from πP\pi_{P}, so the admissible permutations are in one-to-one correspondence with the admissible collections PP of pairs.

Intuitively, the admissible permutations are precisely those permutations that can be obtained by swapping a collection of disjoint pairs (x,y)(x,y) with x<y≤x+5​Dx<y\leq x+5D. For us, such permutations are relevant, because we will alter the bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S we are starting with in our argument via such a permutation π\pi (see also the discussion above), replacing σ\sigma by σ∘π\sigma\circ\pi. More precisely, π\pi will be obtained by composing carefully chosen transposition πb,y\pi_{b,y} (with b<y≤b+5​Db<y\leq b+5D) for each of the elements b∈B⁡(σ)b\in B(\sigma). We will chose these transpositions πb,y\pi_{b,y} one by one for each b∈B⁡(σ)b\in B(\sigma).

For a bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S, an element b∈B⁡(σ)b\in B(\sigma), and an admissible permutation π:{1,…,|S|}→{1,…,|S|}\pi:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to\{1,\dots,|S|\}, let us say that an element y∈{1,…,|S|}y\in\{1,\dots,|S|\} with b<y≤b+5​Db<y\leq b+5D is blocked for σ\sigma, bb and π\pi, if we have Σ⁡(σ∘π∘πb,y,[s,t])=0\Sigma(\sigma\circ\pi\circ\pi_{b,y},[s,t])=0 for some interval [s,t][s,t] with s,t∈{2,…,|S|}s,t\in\{2,\dots,|S|\} and s<ts<t, such that s∈{b+1,…,y}s\in\{b+1,\dots,y\} or t∈{b,…,y−1}t\in\{b,\dots,y-1\}.

Heuristically, if yy is blocked for σ\sigma, bb and π\pi, then this means that we cannot replace σ∘π\sigma\circ\pi by σ∘π∘πb,y\sigma\circ\pi\circ\pi_{b,y} when trying to choose the desired transposition πb,y\pi_{b,y} for the given element b∈B⁡(σ)b\in B(\sigma), because otherwise the interval [s,t][s,t] would create a new problem.

Lemma 5.3.

For a uniformly random bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S, let ℬ3\mathcal{B}_{3} be the event that there exists b∈B⁡(σ)b\in B(\sigma) and an admissible permutation π:{1,…,|S|}→{1,…,|S|}\pi:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to\{1,\dots,|S|\} with {1,…,b−1}⊆Fix⁡(π)\{1,\dots,b-1\}\subseteq\operatorname{Fix}(\pi) such that at least 2​D2D different elements y∈{b+1,…,b+5​D}y\in\{b+1,\dots,b+5D\} are blocked for σ\sigma, bb and π\pi. Then we have ℙ⁡[ℬ3]≤1/25\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}_{3}]\leq 1/25.

We will also postpone the proof of Lemma 5.3 to later (it again uses our anticoncentration results), in order to first see how Theorem 1.2 follows from Lemmas 5.1 to 5.3.

Proof of Lemma 5.1.

ℙ[ℬ1]≤∑b=|S|−30​D|S|ℙ[b∈B(σ)]≤(30​D+1)⋅3|S|α≤100​D(Cα)α≤1100,\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}_{1}]\leq\sum_{b=|S|-30D}^{|S|}\mathbb{P}[b\in B(\sigma)]\leq\frac{(30D+1)\cdot 3}{|S|^{\alpha}}\leq\frac{100D}{(C_{\alpha})^{\alpha}}\leq\frac{1}{100},

as desired. So let b∈{|S|−30​D,…,|S|}b\in\{|S|-30D,\dots,|S|\}, then we have

ℙ[b∈B(σ)]≤∑a=2b−1ℙ[Σ(σ,[a,b])=0]=∑a=2b−1ℙ[σ(a)+⋯+σ(b)=0].\mathbb{P}[b\in B(\sigma)]\leq\sum_{a=2}^{b-1}\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(\sigma,[a,b])=0]=\sum_{a=2}^{b-1}\mathbb{P}[\sigma(a)+\dots+\sigma(b)=0].

For any 2≤a<b≤|S|2\leq a<b\leq|S|, the set {σ⁡(a),…,σ⁡(b)}\{\sigma(a),\dots,\sigma(b)\} is a uniformly random subset of SS of size b−a+1b-a+1. Thus, by Corollary 4.2 (applied with k=1k=1 and m1=b−a+1m_{1}=b-a+1, noting that 2≤m1≤|S|−12\leq m_{1}\leq|S|-1), we have

ℙ[σ(a)+⋯+σ(b)=0]≤(1p+C1​log⁡|S||S|​b−a+1)+(1p+C1​log⁡|S||S|​|S|−b−1+a).\mathbb{P}[\sigma(a)+\dots+\sigma(b)=0]\leq\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{b-a+1}}\Bigg)+\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{|S|-b-1+a}}\Bigg).

Thus, we indeed obtain (recalling that |S|/p≤|S|−α|S|/p\leq|S|^{-\alpha} and 4​C1​log⁡|S|/|S|1/2≤|S|−α4C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}/|S|^{1/2}\leq|S|^{-\alpha})

ℙ[b∈B(σ)]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[b\in B(\sigma)] ≤∑a=2b−1(2p+C1​log⁡|S||S|​b−a+1+C1​log⁡|S||S|​|S|−b−1+a)\displaystyle\leq\sum_{a=2}^{b-1}\Bigg(\frac{2}{p}+\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{b-a+1}}+\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{|S|-b-1+a}}\Bigg)
≤2​|S|p+∑i=2b−1C1​log⁡|S||S|​i+∑i=|S|−b+1|S|−2C1​log⁡|S||S|​i\displaystyle\leq\frac{2|S|}{p}+\sum_{i=2}^{b-1}\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{i}}+\sum_{i=|S|-b+1}^{|S|-2}\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|\sqrt{i}}
≤2​|S|−α+2​C1​log⁡|S||S|​∑i=1|S|1i≤2​|S|−α+4​C1​log⁡|S||S|1/2≤3​|S|−α.∎\displaystyle\leq 2|S|^{-\alpha}+\frac{2C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|}\sum_{i=1}^{|S|}\frac{1}{\sqrt{i}}\leq 2|S|^{-\alpha}+\frac{4C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\leq 3|S|^{-\alpha}.\qed

Before proving Lemmas 5.2 and 5.3, we first prove the following auxiliary lemma.

Lemma 5.4.

For a uniformly random bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S, let ℬ0\mathcal{B}_{0} be the event that for some b∈B⁡(σ)b\in B(\sigma) with b≤|S|−30​Db\leq|S|-30D there exist distinct subsets J,J′⊆{b,b+1,…,b+20​D}J,J^{\prime}\subseteq\{b,b+1,\dots,b+20D\} such that Σ⁡(σ⁡(J))=Σ⁡(σ⁡(J′))\Sigma(\sigma(J))=\Sigma(\sigma(J^{\prime})). Then we have ℙ⁡[ℬ0]≤1/100\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}_{0}]\leq 1/100.

Proof.

It suffices to show that for any b∈{1,…,|S|−30​D}b\in\{1,\dots,|S|-30D\} and any two distinct subsets J,J′⊆{b,b+1,…,b+20​D}J,J^{\prime}\subseteq\{b,b+1,\dots,b+20D\} we have

ℙ[b∈B(σ) and Σ(σ(J))=Σ(σ(J′))]≤8|S|1+α.\mathbb{P}[b\in B(\sigma)\text{ and }\Sigma(\sigma(J))=\Sigma(\sigma(J^{\prime}))]\leq\frac{8}{|S|^{1+\alpha}}. (5.1)

Indeed, given (5.1), taking a union bound over the at most (|S|−30​D)⋅220​D+1⋅220​D+1≤|S|⋅240​D+2(|S|-30D)\cdot 2^{20D+1}\cdot 2^{20D+1}\leq|S|\cdot 2^{40D+2} possibilities for bb, JJ and J′J^{\prime} gives

ℙ⁡[ℬ0]≤|S|⋅240​D+2⋅8|S|1+α=240​D+5|S|α≤240​D+5(Cα)α≤1100.\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}_{0}]\leq|S|\cdot 2^{40D+2}\cdot\frac{8}{|S|^{1+\alpha}}=\frac{2^{40D+5}}{|S|^{\alpha}}\leq\frac{2^{40D+5}}{(C_{\alpha})^{\alpha}}\leq\frac{1}{100}.

So let b∈{1,…,|S|−30​D}b\in\{1,\dots,|S|-30D\}, and consider distinct subsets J,J′⊆{b,b+1,…,b+20​D}J,J^{\prime}\subseteq\{b,b+1,\dots,b+20D\}. Note that the event Σ⁡(σ⁡(J))=Σ⁡(σ⁡(J′))\Sigma(\sigma(J))=\Sigma(\sigma(J^{\prime})) (i.e. the event ∑j∈Jσ⁡(j)=∑j′∈J′σ⁡(j′)\sum_{j\in J}\sigma(j)=\sum_{j^{\prime}\in J^{\prime}}\sigma(j^{\prime})) is determined by the outcomes of σ⁡(b),…,σ⁡(b+20​D)\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(b+20D). Furthermore, choosing an index i∈J​Δ​J′i\in J\Delta J^{\prime} and conditioning on any outcomes of σ⁡(b),…,σ⁡(i−1),σ⁡(i+1),…,σ⁡(b+20​D)\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(i-1),\sigma(i+1),\dots,\sigma(b+20D), we can see that there is at most one outcome for σ⁡(i)\sigma(i) (among the |S|−20​D|S|-20D remaining elements in SS) such that Σ⁡(σ⁡(J))=Σ⁡(σ⁡(J′))\Sigma(\sigma(J))=\Sigma(\sigma(J^{\prime})) is satisfied. Thus, we can conclude

ℙ[Σ(σ(J))=Σ(σ(J′))]≤1|S|−20​D≤2|S|,\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(\sigma(J))=\Sigma(\sigma(J^{\prime}))]\leq\frac{1}{|S|-20D}\leq\frac{2}{|S|},

since |S|≥Cα≥50​D|S|\geq C_{\alpha}\geq 50D. Now, conditioning on any fixed outcomes of σ⁡(b),…,σ⁡(b+20​D)\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(b+20D) such that Σ⁡(σ⁡(J))=Σ⁡(σ⁡(J′))\Sigma(\sigma(J))=\Sigma(\sigma(J^{\prime})) holds, we have

ℙ[b∈B(σ)∣σ(b),…,σ(b+20D)]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[b\in B(\sigma)\mid\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(b+20D)]
≤∑a=2b−1ℙ[Σ(σ,[a,b])=0∣σ(b),…,σ(b+20D)]\displaystyle\qquad\leq\sum_{a=2}^{b-1}\mathbb{P}[\Sigma(\sigma,[a,b])=0\mid\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(b+20D)]
=∑a=2b−1ℙ[σ(a)+⋯+σ(b−1)=−σ(b)∣σ(b),…,σ(b+20D)]\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{a=2}^{b-1}\mathbb{P}[\sigma(a)+\dots+\sigma(b-1)=-\sigma(b)\mid\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(b+20D)]
≤∑a=2b−1(1p+C1​log⁡(|S|−20​D−1)(|S|−20​D−1)​b−a+1p+C1​log⁡(|S|−20​D−1)(|S|−20​D−1)​|S|−20​D−1−b+a),\displaystyle\qquad\leq\sum_{a=2}^{b-1}\Bigg(\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{\log(|S|-20D-1)}}{(|S|-20D-1)\sqrt{b-a}}+\frac{1}{p}+\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{\log(|S|-20D-1)}}{(|S|-20D-1)\sqrt{|S|-20D-1-b+a}}\Bigg),

where in the last step we applied Corollary 4.2 with k=1k=1, noting that conditional on our fixed outcomes of σ⁡(b),…,σ⁡(b+20​D)\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(b+20D), the set {σ⁡(a),…,σ⁡(b−1)}\{\sigma(a),\dots,\sigma(b-1)\} is a uniformly random subset of size b−ab-a in S∖{σ⁡(b),…,σ⁡(b+20​D)}S\setminus\{\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(b+20D)\}. Therefore we can conclude (recalling that |S|≥Cα≥50​D|S|\geq C_{\alpha}\geq 50D as well as |S|/p≤|S|1−α|S|/p\leq|S|^{1-\alpha} and 4​C1​log⁡|S|/|S|1/2≤|S|−α4C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}/|S|^{1/2}\leq|S|^{-\alpha})

ℙ[b∈B(σ)∣σ(b),…,σ(b+20D)]≤2​|S|p+2⋅C1​log⁡|S|(|S|/2)∑i=1|S|1i≤2|S|−α+8​C1​log⁡|S||S|1/2≤4|S|−α\mathbb{P}[b\in B(\sigma)\mid\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(b+20D)]\leq\frac{2|S|}{p}+2\cdot\frac{C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{(|S|/2)}\sum_{i=1}^{|S|}\frac{1}{\sqrt{i}}\leq 2|S|^{-\alpha}+\frac{8C_{1}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\leq 4|S|^{-\alpha}

for any fixed outcomes of σ⁡(b),…,σ⁡(b+20​D)\sigma(b),\dots,\sigma(b+20D). Thus, overall we indeed obtain

ℙ[b∈B(σ) and Σ(σ(J))=Σ(σ(J′))]≤2|S|⋅4|S|−α=8|S|1+α,\mathbb{P}[b\in B(\sigma)\text{ and }\Sigma(\sigma(J))=\Sigma(\sigma(J^{\prime}))]\leq\frac{2}{|S|}\cdot 4|S|^{-\alpha}=\frac{8}{|S|^{1+\alpha}},

proving (5.1) ∎

Now, we are ready to prove Lemma 5.2.

For the events ℬ0\mathcal{B}_{0} and ℬ1\mathcal{B}_{1} in Lemmas 5.4 and 5.1, we have ℙ⁡[ℬ0]≤1/100\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}_{0}]\leq 1/100 and ℙ⁡[ℬ1]≤1/100\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}_{1}]\leq 1/100. As b1,…,bD∈B⁡(σ)b_{1},\dots,b_{D}\in B(\sigma), there are furthermore a1,…,aD∈{2,…,|S|}a_{1},\dots,a_{D}\in\{2,\dots,|S|\} with ai<bia_{i}<b_{i} and Σ⁡(σ,[ai,bi])=0\Sigma(\sigma,[a_{i},b_{i}])=0 for i=1,…,Di=1,\dots,D. We claim that a1,…,aDa_{1},\dots,a_{D} must be distinct. Indeed, assume that ai=aha_{i}=a_{h} for two distinct i,h∈{1,…,D}i,h\in\{1,\dots,D\}, and assume without loss of generality that bi<bhb_{i}<b_{h}. Now we have

This means that ℬ0\mathcal{B}_{0} holds, which is a contradiction. Therefore a1,…,aDa_{1},\dots,a_{D} must indeed be distinct.

We may now assume without loss of generality that a1<⋯<aDa_{1}<\dots<a_{D}. We also claim that aD<b0a_{D}<b_{0}. Indeed, if aD≥b0a_{D}\geq b_{0} we would have b0≤aD<bD≤b0+20​Db_{0}\leq a_{D}<b_{D}\leq b_{0}+20D and furthermore Σ⁡(σ⁡({aD,…,bD}))=Σ⁡(σ,[aD,bD])=0\Sigma(\sigma(\{a_{D},\dots,b_{D}\}))=\Sigma(\sigma,[a_{D},b_{D}])=0. Thus, considering b0∈B⁡(σ)b_{0}\in B(\sigma) and J={aD,…,bD}⊆{b0,…,b0+20​D}J=\{a_{D},\dots,b_{D}\}\subseteq\{b_{0},\dots,b_{0}+20D\} we would again have J≠∅J\neq\emptyset, but Σ⁡(σ⁡(J))=0=Σ⁡(σ⁡(∅))\Sigma(\sigma(J))=0=\Sigma(\sigma(\emptyset)). So again ℬ0\mathcal{B}_{0} would hold, contradicting our assumption that ℬ2∖(ℬ0∪ℬ1)\mathcal{B}_{2}\setminus(\mathcal{B}_{0}\cup\mathcal{B}_{1}) holds.

Therefore we must have aD<b0a_{D}<b_{0} and hence a1<⋯<aD<b0a_{1}<\dots<a_{D}<b_{0}. Summarizing this, we found that if ℬ2∖(ℬ0∪ℬ1)\mathcal{B}_{2}\setminus(\mathcal{B}_{0}\cup\mathcal{B}_{1}) holds, there must exist b0∈{1,…,|S|−30​D}b_{0}\in\{1,\dots,|S|-30D\} and b1,…,bD∈{b0+1,…,b0+20​D}b_{1},\dots,b_{D}\in\{b_{0}+1,\dots,b_{0}+20D\} as well as a1,…,aD∈{1,…,|S|}a_{1},\dots,a_{D}\in\{1,\dots,|S|\} with a1<⋯<aD<b0a_{1}<\dots<a_{D}<b_{0} such that Σ⁡(σ,[ai,bi])=0\Sigma(\sigma,[a_{i},b_{i}])=0 for i=1,…,Di=1,\dots,D.

For any given b0∈{1,…,|S|−30​D}b_{0}\in\{1,\dots,|S|-30D\} and b1,…,bD∈{b0+1,…,b0+20​D}b_{1},\dots,b_{D}\in\{b_{0}+1,\dots,b_{0}+20D\}, conditioning on any fixed outcomes of σ⁡(b0),…,σ⁡(b0+20​D)\sigma(b_{0}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}+20D), we have

ℙ[there are a1<⋯<aD<b0 with Σ(σ,[ai,bi])=0 for i=1,…,D|σ(b0),…,σ(b0+20D)]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big[\text{there are }a_{1}<\dots<a_{D}<b_{0}\text{ with }\Sigma(\sigma,[a_{i},b_{i}])=0\text{ for }i=1,\dots,D\,\Big|\,\sigma(b_{0}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}+20D)\Big]
≤∑1≤a1<⋯<aD<b0ℙ[Σ(σ,[ai,bi])=0 for i=1,…,D|σ(b0),…,σ(b0+20D)]\displaystyle\qquad\leq\sum_{1\leq a_{1}<\dots<a_{D}<b_{0}}\mathbb{P}\Big[\Sigma(\sigma,[a_{i},b_{i}])=0\text{ for }i=1,\dots,D\,\Big|\,\sigma(b_{0}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}+20D)\Big]

Each term on the right-hand side can be bounded by Corollary 4.2, noting that Σ⁡(σ,[ai,b0−1])=Σ⁡({σ⁡(ai),…,σ⁡(b0−1)})\Sigma(\sigma,[a_{i},b_{0}-1])=\Sigma(\{\sigma(a_{i}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}-1)\}) for i=1,…,Di=1,\dots,D, and that {σ⁡(aD),…,σ⁡(b0−1)}⊆⋯⊆{σ⁡(a1),…,σ⁡(b0−1)}\{\sigma(a_{D}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}-1)\}\subseteq\dots\subseteq\{\sigma(a_{1}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}-1)\} (conditional on our fixed outcomes of σ⁡(b0),…,σ⁡(b0+20​D)\sigma(b_{0}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}+20D)) is a uniformly random chain of subsets of S∖{σ⁡(b0),…,σ⁡(b0+20​D)}S\setminus\{\sigma(b_{0}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}+20D)\} of sizes b0−aD,…,b0−a1b_{0}-a_{D},\dots,b_{0}-a_{1}, where 1≤b0−aD<⋯<b0−a1<|S|−20​D−11\leq b_{0}-a_{D}<\dots<b_{0}-a_{1}<|S|-20D-1. ℙ[there are a1<⋯<aD<b0 with Σ(σ,[ai,bi])=0 for i=1,…,D|σ(b0),…,σ(b0+20D)]\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big[\text{there are }a_{1}<\dots<a_{D}<b_{0}\text{ with }\Sigma(\sigma,[a_{i},b_{i}])=0\text{ for }i=1,\dots,D\,\Big|\,\sigma(b_{0}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}+20D)\Big]
≤(D+1)⋅(|S|−20​D−1p+2​CD​log⁡(|S|−20​D−1)(|S|−20​D−1)1/2)D\displaystyle\qquad\leq(D+1)\cdot\Bigg(\frac{|S|-20D-1}{p}+\frac{2C_{D}\sqrt{\log(|S|-20D-1)}}{(|S|-20D-1)^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{D}
≤(D+1)⋅(|S|p+4​CD​log⁡|S||S|1/2)D≤(D+1)⋅(2​|S|−α)D=(D+1)​2D⋅|S|−α​D≤(D+1)​2D|S|3\displaystyle\qquad\leq(D+1)\cdot\Bigg(\frac{|S|}{p}+\frac{4C_{D}\sqrt{\log|S|}}{|S|^{1/2}}\Bigg)^{D}\leq(D+1)\cdot(2|S|^{-\alpha})^{D}=(D+1)2^{D}\cdot|S|^{-\alpha D}\leq\frac{(D+1)2^{D}}{|S|^{3}}

for any given b0∈{1,…,|S|−30​D}b_{0}\in\{1,\dots,|S|-30D\} and b1,…,bD∈{b0+1,…,b0+20​D}b_{1},\dots,b_{D}\in\{b_{0}+1,\dots,b_{0}+20D\}, and any fixed outcomes of σ⁡(b0),…,σ⁡(b0+20​D)\sigma(b_{0}),\dots,\sigma(b_{0}+20D). This shows that

for any b0∈{1,…,|S|−30​D}b_{0}\in\{1,\dots,|S|-30D\} and b1,…,bD∈{b0+1,…,b0+20​D}b_{1},\dots,b_{D}\in\{b_{0}+1,\dots,b_{0}+20D\}. To prove Lemma 5.3, we also need another auxiliary lemma.

Lemma 5.5.

Let b,b′∈{2,…​|S|−2}b,b^{\prime}\in\{2,\dots|S|-2\} with b′−b=5​Db^{\prime}-b=5D, let u1,…,uD∈{b,…,b′}u_{1},\dots,u_{D}\in\{b,\dots,b^{\prime}\}, and consider permutations π1,…,πD:{1,…,|S|}→{1,…,|S|}\pi_{1},\dots,\pi_{D}:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to\{1,\dots,|S|\} with {1,…,b−1}∪{b′+1,…,|S|}⊆Fix⁡(πi)\{1,\dots,b-1\}\cup\{b^{\prime}+1,\dots,|S|\}\subseteq\operatorname{Fix}(\pi_{i}) for i=1,…,Di=1,\dots,D. Then, for a uniformly random bijection σ:{1,…,|S|}→S\sigma:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to S, it happens with probability at most 1/|S|21/|S|^{2} that there exist x1,…,xD∈{b′+1,…,|S|}x_{1},\dots,x_{D}\in\{b^{\prime}+1,\dots,|S|\} with x1<⋯<xDx_{1}<\dots<x_{D}, as well as an admissible permutation π:{1,…,|S|}→{1,…,|S|}\pi:\{1,\dots,|S|\}\to\{1,\dots,|S|\}, such that Σ⁡(σ∘π∘πi,[ui,xi])=0\Sigma(\sigma\circ\pi\circ\pi_{i},[u_{i},x_{i}])=0 for i=1,…,Di=1,\dots,D.

By flipping the ordering of {1,…,|S|}\{1,\dots,|S|\}, we obtain the following analogous statement from Lemma 5.5.

Lemma 5.6.
